messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

James, a 58-year-old African American hairdresser, has been struggling with persistent thoughts and reactions stemming from a traumatic mugging that occurred six months ago. On that fateful night, James was closing up his salon when two individuals, one of whom had a strong odor of alcohol, entered the shop. They acted suspiciously and quickly overpowered him, leaving him feeling helpless and humiliated. Ever since, specific triggers have made it difficult for James to function normally. James's experience has left him with vivid visual memories that replay like a film whenever he encounters certain triggers, such as people acting suspiciously or the smell of alcohol. These intrusive images are so powerful that they often render him speechless and unable to articulate what happened. What frightens him most is not just the memory itself but the sense of helplessness it brings back. He finds himself constantly on edge, anticipating another encounter with someone who might act suspiciously. James has come to believe that he was somehow at fault for the mugging—that if only he had been more alert or taken different precautions, he could have avoided the situation. This self-blame has led him to dwell endlessly on what he did wrong and try hard not to think about the trauma itself. As a result, James has become increasingly isolated, avoiding social interactions that might trigger these thoughts. His occupation as a hairdresser, which once brought him joy and satisfaction, now feels like a minefield of potential triggers. The alcohol smell from colognes or perfumes used by his clients often brings back vivid images of the mugger, leaving him feeling overwhelmed and unable to focus on his work. Similarly, any client who appears nervous or anxious can set off a chain reaction of memories that make it difficult for James to provide the care and attention he once did. The more James avoids these triggers, the stronger they seem to become. He finds himself increasingly suspicious of people around him, and this has strained his relationships at work and home. His wife notices how he becomes tense and withdrawn in social settings, and even small criticisms from clients can send him into a spiral of self-blame and rumination. James’s memory of the trauma is so vivid that it feels like he relives the event over and over again. This constant replaying of the incident reinforces his tendency to blame himself and avoid situations where he might be reminded of the mugging. Even simple tasks, such as closing up the salon at night or walking home from work, have become sources of significant anxiety. The weight of these experiences has made James realize that he needs help. His self-imposed isolation has affected not only his job but also his marriage and overall well-being. He is most afraid of reliving the trauma again, but he hopes that with support, he can regain control over his life and find a way to manage his memories without letting them dominate his existence. James's journey towards seeking help reflects a growing awareness that his current strategies are not sustainable. The triggers, maladaptive thoughts, and intrusive memories have created a self-reinforcing cycle that has only intensified over time. He is now determined to break this pattern and find a way to live more fully without the constant fear of another traumatic encounter.
